subtopic_detail: classifying recurrent disproportionate aggression that resolves completely between episodes in an otherwise law abiding adult
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 29 year old man referred by his general practitioner after he punched a hole in a plasterboard wall when his internet connection dropped during a video call.

He describes roughly fortnightly episodes over the past three years in which he becomes enraged within seconds over something he later agrees was trivial, shouts, and sometimes throws or breaks an object. The episodes last under twenty minutes and he is remorseful and embarrassed afterwards. Between episodes his mood is stable and he is described by his partner as gentle. He has never been arrested, does not deceive people or take their belongings, has never harmed an animal, and had no behavioural difficulties at school. He drinks two beers on Fridays and uses no other substances. He has no head injury, no seizures and no memory gaps around the episodes.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination normal between episodes with euthymic mood, reactive affect, no psychotic phenomena, no cognitive impairment, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and urine drug screen all within normal limits, electroencephalogram reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Antisocial personality disorder with a predominantly aggressive presentation
options.rationale: This diagnosis requires a pervasive pattern of disregard for the rights of others since age fifteen, including deceitfulness, unlawful behaviour and absent remorse, with evidence of conduct disorder before age fifteen. He was well behaved at school, has no criminal history and is consistently remorseful, which excludes it. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Bipolar affective disorder with recurrent irritable hypomanic episodes occurring
options.rationale: Hypomania requires a sustained period of at least four consecutive days of abnormally elevated or irritable mood with increased energy and associated features such as reduced need for sleep and increased goal directed activity. His episodes last minutes rather than days and his mood is entirely normal between them. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Intermittent explosive disorder with recurrent impulsive aggressive outbursts
options.rationale: Recurrent outbursts of aggression grossly out of proportion to the provocation, impulsive rather than premeditated, not committed for any tangible gain, and occurring in someone whose functioning is normal between episodes, is precisely this diagnosis. The frequency criterion of verbal or minor physical aggression roughly twice weekly for three months, or three episodes of destruction or injury within a year, is met by three years of fortnightly destructive episodes. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Borderline personality disorder with affective instability and anger dyscontrol
options.rationale: Inappropriate intense anger is one of its criteria, so this is a genuine near miss, and the diagnosis also requires a pervasive pattern of unstable relationships, identity disturbance, abandonment fears, self harm and chronic emptiness. He has a stable relationship, a stable sense of self and no self harm, so the anger stands alone rather than sitting within a broader pattern. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Focal epilepsy of temporal lobe origin presenting with episodic ictal aggression
options.rationale: Ictal aggression is rare, undirected and stereotyped, and it is accompanied by impaired awareness, automatisms and postictal confusion with amnesia for the event. He has clear recall, directed behaviour, full awareness throughout and a normal electroencephalogram. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

explanation.summary: Intermittent explosive disorder is defined by recurrent failure to resist aggressive impulses, with outbursts grossly disproportionate to the provocation, impulsive rather than planned, and not undertaken for any tangible objective such as money or intimidation. The essential discriminator is that functioning between episodes is entirely normal, which separates it from personality disorders where the disturbance is pervasive and from mood disorders where the abnormality is sustained. Remorse after the event is characteristic and argues against antisocial personality disorder. Organic causes including epilepsy, head injury and substance intoxication must be excluded before the diagnosis is made. Cognitive behavioural therapy focused on relaxation, cognitive restructuring and relapse prevention is first line, with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors having the best pharmacological evidence.
key_points: Outbursts are impulsive, disproportionate to provocation, and not committed for tangible gain.
Normal functioning between episodes distinguishes it from personality and mood disorders.
Remorse and embarrassment after episodes argue against antisocial personality disorder.
Organic causes including epilepsy, head injury and substance use must be excluded first.
Cognitive behavioural therapy is first line, with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors the best evidenced medication.
explanation.pearls: Establish what the person is like between episodes before diagnosing an anger problem, because completely normal interepisode functioning with genuine remorse points to intermittent explosive disorder, whereas pervasive instability across relationships and identity points to a personality disorder instead.

sources.label: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

subtopic_detail: distinguishing genuine autobiographical memory loss from feigned amnesia when a financial motive is present
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 44 year old man brought to the emergency department by police after being found wandering in a coastal town three hundred kilometres from his home.

He cannot recall his name, his address or anything about his personal history, and he appears genuinely distressed by this. He is oriented to place and time, can tell you the date and the name of the prime minister, drove himself there and can operate his phone, read the newspaper and describe how to make a cup of tea. His wife arrives and tells you he had been served with bankruptcy papers the day before he disappeared and that his father died by suicide in similar financial circumstances. Computed tomography of his head is normal, his ethanol level is zero and his urine drug screen is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and cooperative, distressed affect, no thought disorder or psychotic phenomena, cranial nerves and peripheral neurological examination normal, no head injury, Mini Mental State Examination 29 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography of the head normal, ethanol zero, urine drug screen negative, electrolytes, glucose, liver function, thyroid function and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Wernicke encephalopathy with confabulation from thiamine deficiency
options.rationale: Wernicke encephalopathy presents with some combination of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, usually with a history of alcohol dependence or malnutrition, and the amnesia that follows it is anterograde with confabulation. His cranial nerves and gait are normal, his ethanol is zero and he is forming new memories perfectly well. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue following overwhelming stress
options.rationale: Loss of autobiographical and identity memory with wholly intact semantic and procedural memory, purposeful travel away from home, and an immediately preceding overwhelming psychological stressor is the defining pattern of this disorder, and organic causes have been excluded. The financial motive raises malingering properly, but a malingerer typically presents with a vague global memory loss rather than this sharply selective sparing of skills, and genuine distress with a personally significant precipitant supports a dissociative process. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Transient global amnesia with dense anterograde memory loss and repeated questioning
options.rationale: Transient global amnesia causes profound anterograde memory failure with repetitive questioning, preserved personal identity and resolution within twenty four hours. He knows the date and can form new memories, and crucially it is his identity that is lost, which transient global amnesia characteristically spares. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Malingered amnesia motivated by avoidance of impending bankruptcy proceedings
options.rationale: External incentive is present and must be weighed seriously, but malingering is a diagnosis of exclusion that requires positive evidence such as inconsistent performance, dramatic presentation on demand or symptoms that do not follow any known memory architecture. His deficit is neuropsychologically coherent, he is distressed rather than indifferent, and the amnesia itself does nothing to prevent the bankruptcy proceeding. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Non convulsive status epilepticus producing a prolonged postictal confusional state
options.rationale: Non convulsive status causes fluctuating conscious state, impaired attention and automatisms, and it would be detected on electroencephalography. He is fully alert with intact attention and orientation, performing complex purposeful tasks such as driving and using his phone. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

explanation.summary: Dissociative amnesia involves an inability to recall important autobiographical information, usually of a traumatic or stressful nature, that is too extensive to be ordinary forgetting and is not explained by a substance or neurological condition. The fugue subtype adds purposeful travel or wandering with confusion about identity. The diagnostic signature is dissociation between memory systems: autobiographical and identity memory are lost while semantic knowledge, procedural skills and the ability to form new memories remain fully intact. Organic causes must be excluded, which is what the imaging, toxicology and biochemistry accomplish here. Malingering deserves serious consideration whenever there is an external incentive, but it is not diagnosed merely because an incentive exists, and it requires positive evidence of feigning rather than the coherent selective pattern seen here.
key_points: Autobiographical and identity memory are lost while semantic and procedural memory remain intact.
Dissociative fugue adds purposeful travel away from home with confusion about identity.
Organic causes including head injury, substances, seizures and thiamine deficiency must be excluded first.
Transient global amnesia spares identity and causes dense anterograde failure with repetitive questioning.
Malingering requires positive evidence of feigning, not merely the presence of an external incentive.
explanation.pearls: Test procedural and semantic memory separately from autobiographical memory in any presentation of amnesia, because preserved ability to drive, read and name the prime minister alongside a lost identity is the pattern of dissociative amnesia, whereas feigned amnesia is usually globally and implausibly dense.

sources.label: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

subtopic_detail: establishing the nature of frequent prolonged events that have not responded to escalating anticonvulsant treatment
stem:
You are the neuropsychiatry registrar seeing a 24 year old woman referred with events occurring up to four times a week for two years. She has been treated with three anticonvulsants at therapeutic doses without any reduction in frequency.

Her partner has recorded one on a phone. During the event she lies on the floor with her eyes tightly closed, her head turns rapidly from side to side, and her limbs move in an irregular asynchronous way that waxes and wanes over nine minutes. She resists having her eyelids opened. She has never been incontinent, has never bitten her tongue and has never been injured. Afterwards she is tearful but immediately oriented and can describe the room throughout. Her magnetic resonance imaging is normal, her routine interictal electroencephalograms have been normal, and her serum lactate taken twenty minutes after one event was normal.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal between events, normal gait and coordination, mental state shows anxious affect with no psychotic phenomena, no cognitive impairment
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain normal, three routine interictal electroencephalograms normal, serum lactate normal twenty minutes after a witnessed event, electrolytes glucose and calcium within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Video electroencephalography telemetry to capture a typical event
options.rationale: Simultaneous video and electroencephalographic recording of a habitual event is the only way to establish whether the behaviour is accompanied by an ictal electrographic discharge, and it is the accepted standard for this diagnosis. Routine interictal studies cannot settle the question because they are frequently normal between genuine seizures as well, so capturing an event is what distinguishes the two. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Add a fourth anticonvulsant and reassess the frequency after three months
options.rationale: Adding further anticonvulsants is what happens to these patients for years before diagnosis, exposing them to teratogenic risk, cognitive adverse effects and occasionally intubation for presumed status epilepticus. Failure of three appropriately dosed drugs should prompt a review of the diagnosis rather than a fourth trial. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Repeat the magnetic resonance imaging using a dedicated epilepsy protocol
options.rationale: A dedicated epilepsy protocol does improve detection of hippocampal sclerosis and focal cortical dysplasia and is worthwhile in drug resistant focal epilepsy. It cannot determine whether these particular events are epileptic, and a structural lesion would not by itself explain semiology this atypical. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Measure serum prolactin immediately after the next witnessed event occurs
options.rationale: Prolactin rises after generalised tonic clonic seizures and was formerly used this way, and its sensitivity is poor, it is unhelpful after focal seizures, and it must be drawn within a narrow window against a baseline. A normal result would not exclude epilepsy and so cannot establish the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Arrange cardiac monitoring with a prolonged implantable loop recorder inserted
options.rationale: Loop recorders are used where unexplained transient loss of consciousness may be arrhythmic, typically with abrupt collapse, brief duration and rapid full recovery. Nine minutes of asynchronous movement with retained awareness throughout does not fit a cardiac mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

explanation.summary: Psychogenic non epileptic seizures account for a substantial minority of patients referred to epilepsy services and are typically diagnosed after years of ineffective anticonvulsant treatment. Several features in the recorded event favour a non epileptic mechanism: forced eye closure with resistance to passive opening, side to side head movement, asynchronous limb movements that wax and wane, prolonged duration beyond a few minutes, retained awareness throughout, and the absence of tongue biting, incontinence or injury. A normal postictal lactate also argues against a generalised convulsion. None of these features is individually decisive, which is why video electroencephalography telemetry capturing a habitual event is the diagnostic standard. Diagnosis matters because the treatment is psychological therapy rather than anticonvulsants, and because these patients are otherwise at risk of harmful escalation including intubation for presumed status epilepticus.
key_points: Forced eye closure with resistance to opening is uncommon in epileptic seizures.
Asynchronous waxing and waning movements lasting beyond a few minutes favour a non epileptic mechanism.
Retained awareness with immediate orientation afterwards argues against a generalised convulsion.
Normal interictal electroencephalography occurs in genuine epilepsy and cannot exclude or confirm the diagnosis.
Treatment is psychological therapy, and anticonvulsants should be withdrawn once the diagnosis is secure.
explanation.pearls: Treat failure of three appropriately dosed anticonvulsants as a reason to question the diagnosis rather than to add a fourth, and arrange video telemetry, because these patients are otherwise escalated for years and occasionally intubated for presumed status epilepticus.

subtopic_detail: reconsidering a long standing anxiety label in a woman whose exhaustion follows social effort rather than preceding it
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 31 year old woman referred after a third trial of a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor failed to help what has been treated as social anxiety disorder since she was nineteen.

She describes rehearsing conversations in advance, keeping a mental list of topics, and copying the facial expressions of colleagues so she appears normal. She says she is not frightened of being judged but finds the effort of appearing natural exhausting, and she sleeps for most of Saturday after a working week. She has an encyclopaedic knowledge of eighteenth century textiles and can talk about them at length. She reports that unexpected changes to plans leave her unable to function for the rest of the day, that certain clothing labels are unbearable against her skin, and that she has always counted steps when walking.

data_table.Examination: Limited spontaneous eye contact with effortful compensation, precise formal speech, mood euthymic, no psychotic phenomena, no compulsions performed to neutralise a feared outcome
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, thyroid function and iron studies within normal limits, previous trials of sertraline, escitalopram and venlafaxine each at adequate dose and duration without benefit

lead_in: What is the most likely explanation for her presentation?

options.text: Treatment resistant social anxiety disorder requiring augmentation of her medication
options.rationale: Social anxiety disorder is driven by fear of negative evaluation and humiliation, and she explicitly denies fear of judgement, describing instead the effort of appearing natural. Three adequate medication trials without benefit is itself evidence that the original formulation was wrong rather than that more medication is needed. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Obsessive compulsive disorder with counting compulsions and an intense special interest
options.rationale: Compulsions in obsessive compulsive disorder are performed to neutralise a specific feared outcome and are experienced as unwanted and ego dystonic, whereas her counting and her textile interest are neither distressing nor aimed at preventing anything. The examination explicitly notes no compulsions performed to neutralise a feared outcome. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Autism spectrum disorder with camouflaging that has delayed her diagnosis
options.rationale: Rehearsing scripts, maintaining topic lists and consciously imitating the expressions of others is camouflaging, an effortful compensation that masks social communication difficulty and is far commoner in women, which is why they are diagnosed later and more often misdiagnosed with anxiety. The exhaustion following social effort rather than preceding it, alongside insistence on sameness, sensory sensitivity to clothing labels and a circumscribed intense interest, completes the diagnostic picture. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Schizoid personality disorder with restricted affect and a preference for solitude
options.rationale: Schizoid personality disorder involves genuine indifference to relationships and little desire for social contact, so the person makes no effort to fit in. She works hard to appear natural and finds it costly, which indicates that she wants social connection and lacks the intuitive means rather than lacking the desire. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Persistent depressive disorder producing fatigue, low motivation and social withdrawal
options.rationale: Chronic depression would involve pervasive low mood with anhedonia over at least two years, and her mood is euthymic on examination and she retains intense pleasure in her special interest. Her fatigue follows social effort specifically rather than being present regardless of activity. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

explanation.summary: Autistic women are diagnosed substantially later than men, frequently after years of treatment for anxiety, depression or an eating disorder, because camouflaging conceals the social communication differences that diagnostic criteria were originally written to capture in boys. Camouflaging means consciously masking difficulty through rehearsed scripts, imitated expressions and prepared conversational material, and it is effortful in a way that produces characteristic exhaustion after social contact rather than anticipatory fear before it. That distinction is the key discriminator from social anxiety disorder, where the fear is of negative evaluation and precedes the encounter. The restricted and repetitive domain is present here as insistence on sameness, sensory sensitivity and a circumscribed intense interest. Recognition matters because it redirects care from repeated medication trials towards environmental adjustment, sensory accommodation and appropriate support.
key_points: Camouflaging masks social communication difference and is markedly more common in autistic women.
Exhaustion after social effort distinguishes camouflaging from the anticipatory fear of social anxiety disorder.
The restricted and repetitive domain includes insistence on sameness, sensory sensitivity and circumscribed interests.
Autistic special interests are pleasurable and ego syntonic, unlike the distressing compulsions of obsessive compulsive disorder.
Repeated failure of adequate medication trials should prompt review of the formulation rather than further augmentation.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the fear comes before the social event or the exhaustion comes after it, because anticipatory fear of judgement points to social anxiety disorder while post social depletion from effortful masking points to undiagnosed autism, and the distinction redirects care away from a fourth antidepressant trial.

sources.label: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition
Autism CRC: National Guideline for Autism Assessment

subtopic_detail: identifying the disorder behind repeated presentations for infant reassurance when screening for low mood is negative
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29 year old woman with her 10 week old first baby. This is her fifth visit in three weeks, each time about a different symptom in the baby that has resolved by the time she arrives.

She describes checking the baby's breathing between eight and ten times each night and lying awake listening to the monitor even when the baby is asleep and settled. She has intrusive images of the baby stopping breathing that she finds horrifying and wholly unwanted, and she has never had any thought of harming the baby herself. She says her mood is fine, she enjoys the baby, she laughs with her partner and she looks forward to her mothers group. She is eating normally but is exhausted. Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 11, with the three anxiety items accounting for most of it and item 10 scored zero.

data_table.Examination: Appears tired but engaged, interacts warmly and responsively with the baby, mood euthymic with reactive affect, no psychotic phenomena, no thoughts of harm to self or the baby
data_table.Investigations: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale 11 with item 10 scored zero, full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function all within normal limits, baby thriving on the 50th centile with a normal examination

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Postnatal anxiety disorder with prominent checking and intrusive unwanted images
options.rationale: Perinatal anxiety is at least as common as perinatal depression and frequently presents as repeated health seeking for the infant, excessive checking and unwanted intrusive images of harm coming to the baby, in a woman whose mood is preserved. Her Edinburgh score of 11 driven by the three anxiety items with a normal mood and preserved enjoyment fits an anxiety disorder rather than a depressive one, and the intrusive images are egodystonic and therefore not a risk to the baby. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Postnatal depression that the screening tool has partially failed to capture
options.rationale: Her total score is above the usual referral threshold, which makes this worth considering, and the diagnosis requires persistent low mood or loss of interest, and she reports preserved mood, preserved enjoyment of the baby and preserved social engagement. The elevated score comes specifically from the anxiety items rather than the depressive ones. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Postpartum psychosis with delusional beliefs about the baby's physical health
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is an emergency presenting within days to weeks with delusions, hallucinations, confusion and rapidly fluctuating mood, and it requires urgent admission. Her beliefs are not held with conviction, she recognises the images as unwanted products of her own mind, and there are no psychotic phenomena. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Factitious disorder imposed on another with fabricated symptoms in the infant
options.rationale: This involves deliberate falsification or induction of illness in the child to obtain attention through the sick role, and the presenting adult is typically calm and comfortable in medical settings. She is genuinely distressed, is seeking reassurance rather than investigation, and the baby has no fabricated findings. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Normal adjustment to first time parenthood requiring reassurance and sleep support
options.rationale: Some vigilance and worry is entirely normal in new parents, and this has crossed into disorder because it is producing insomnia when the baby sleeps, five medical presentations in three weeks and marked distress. Normalising it would leave a treatable condition untreated and reinforce the reassurance seeking. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

explanation.summary: Perinatal anxiety is at least as common as perinatal depression and is far more often missed, partly because screening and public awareness both centre on low mood. It commonly presents as repeated presentations about the infant, compulsive checking of breathing, inability to sleep when the baby sleeps, and unwanted intrusive images of harm befalling the baby. Those intrusive images are egodystonic, meaning the mother finds them horrifying and alien, which distinguishes them from the egosyntonic delusional beliefs of postpartum psychosis and means they do not indicate risk to the infant. Examining the subscale structure of the Edinburgh scale rather than the total score alone is what reveals the anxiety pattern here, with item 10 confirming absence of self harm thoughts. Treatment is psychological, with cognitive behavioural therapy first line and medication reserved for more severe or non responsive presentations.
key_points: Perinatal anxiety is at least as common as perinatal depression and is more frequently missed.
Items 3, 4 and 5 of the Edinburgh scale form an anxiety subscale that can drive an elevated total score.
Item 10 specifically screens for thoughts of self harm and must always be reviewed individually.
Egodystonic intrusive images of harm are distressing to the mother and do not indicate risk to the infant.
Cognitive behavioural therapy is first line, with medication reserved for severe or non responsive illness.
explanation.pearls: Ask a mother with intrusive thoughts of harm whether the thought is horrifying to her or feels reasonable, because egodystonic unwanted images indicate an anxiety disorder that responds to therapy while egosyntonic beliefs about the baby suggest psychosis requiring urgent admission.

sources.label: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline
